intent_en: To explain the differing stability of the East and West Antarctic ice sheets in response to climate change, highlighting the vulnerability of the West due to its below-sea-level topography.
previous_intent: To explain the differing vulnerability of the eastern and western Antarctic ice sheets to climate change, highlighting that the western region is more prone to rapid collapse due to its location below sea level.
narration_support: The eastern ice sheet lies mostly on high ground... remains relatively stable. But Western Antarctica is different. Most of it lies below sea level. That means, as it thins, water can undermine it, possibly kick-starting a more rapid collapse.
chart_support: Cross-section chart showing elevation versus distance, depicting the ice sheet and bedrock profile with significant portions of the bedrock lying below sea level.
evidence_note: The narration explicitly contrasts the high ground of the East with the below-sea-level terrain of the West, and the chart visualizes this elevation difference with bedrock dipping below the sea level line.
